source: Year 12 Physics Projectile Motion Problem Set
text: Elevated Launch into the OceanUse g = 9.80 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance unless otherwise stated. Take upwards as positive. A coastal defense battery fires a test projectile from the edge of a cliff 32.0 m above sea level. The projectile is launched with an initial speed of 24.0 m s^(−1) at an angle of 35.0^(∘) above the horizontal. (a) Determine the initial horizontal and vertical components of the launch velocity. (2 marks) (b) Calculate the maximum height reached by the projectile above sea level. (2 marks) (c) Calculate the total time of flight before the projectile strikes the water. (3 marks) (d) Find the horizontal range from the base of the cliff to the impact site. (2 marks) (e) Determine the magnitude and direction of the velocity vector immediately prior to impact with the water. (3 marks)
sourceReviewNotes: Full-precision rounding check: the horizontal range is 84.9453 m, or 84.9 m to three significant figures. The supplied key rounds intermediate values and reports 85.0 m. Accept a consistent calculation near 85.0 m.

text: Clearing an ObstacleUse g = 9.80 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance unless otherwise stated. Take upwards as positive. During a training simulation, a rugby ball is kicked from ground level with an initial velocity of 28.5 m s^(−1) at an angle of 42.0^(∘) to the horizontal. A defensive training barrier of height 12.0 m is positioned 55.0 m horizontally downfield from the kick location. (a) Show by calculation whether the ball clears the defensive barrier, and determine the vertical clearance margin. (4 marks) (b) State whether the ball is ascending or descending as it passes over the barrier. Justify your answer with an explicit velocity calculation. (2 marks) (c) Calculate the horizontal distance from the barrier to where the ball lands on the level ground. (3 marks)
sourceReviewNotes: Full-precision rounding check: the clearance is 4.47882 m, or 4.48 m to three significant figures. The supplied key rounds intermediate values and reports 4.47 m.

text: Horizontal Launch onto an Inclined PlaneUse g = 9.80 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance. State a consistent vertical sign convention. A rescue flare is fired horizontally at 15.0 m s^(−1) from the edge of a uniform hillside that slopes downwards at a constant angle of 30.0^(∘) below the horizontal. (a) Write parametric equations for the horizontal displacement x(t) and vertical displacement y(t) as functions of time t, taking the launch point as the origin (0,0). (2 marks) (b) By equating the trajectory to the geometry of the incline, calculate the time elapsed from launch until the flare strikes the slope. (3 marks) (c) Calculate the straight-line distance along the slope from the launch point to the point of impact. (2 marks)

text: Aeroplane Supply DropFor parts (a)–(c), use g = 9.80 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance. Part (d) considers air resistance. Take upwards as positive. A humanitarian transport aeroplane is descending at a constant angle of 20.0^(∘) below the horizontal at a speed of 85.0 m s^(−1). When the aeroplane is at an altitude of 450 m, an emergency supply container is released from the cargo bay. (a) State the initial horizontal and vertical velocity components of the container at the instant of release. (2 marks) (b) Calculate the total time taken for the container to strike the ground. (3 marks) (c) Calculate the horizontal distance travelled by the container between release and ground impact. (2 marks) (d) In real atmospheric conditions, the supply container experiences non-negligible air resistance. Explain qualitatively how air resistance would affect: (3 marks) ☐ The horizontal velocity throughout the descent. ☐ The total time of flight compared to the ideal theoretical value. ☐ The final angle of impact relative to the horizontal.
